questions.prompt: What does one buffer-pool frame contain in the lecture’s model?
options: A directory entry instead of page bytes
One page
Exactly one record, even if smaller than a page
An entire logical file regardless of size
questions.explanation: A frame holds a page. That page may contain several records.

questions.prompt: May a frame with pinCount=2 be selected as a victim merely because it is very old?
options: Yes, if it is clean
Yes, if it is dirty
No
Yes; LRU always prioritises age
questions.explanation: A nonzero pin count forbids replacement in this model. Being clean does not make an in-use page safe to evict.

questions.prompt: What does the dirty flag indicate?
options: At least one caller is currently using the page
The page was referenced during a recent CLOCK sweep
The page contains a record failing a predicate
The RAM page has modifications not yet reflected in its persistent copy
questions.explanation: Dirty state tracks modifications. Access frequency and pinning use different metadata.

questions.prompt: Why maintain a hash table mapping PageId to a RAM frame?
options: To locate cached pages quickly
To precompute every query result
To sort disk pages by search key
To replace all pin and dirty metadata
questions.explanation: Frequent page lookups need to be fast. The mapping does not change relational data.

questions.prompt: Does unpinning a page down to pinCount=0 force immediate eviction?
options: It can never be evicted again
No; it only becomes eligible for replacement
Yes; it is always removed immediately
Yes, if it was just read
questions.explanation: With no current user, the page becomes eligible, but the policy may keep it for reuse.

questions.prompt: A cached page has pinCount=1. What happens when it is pinned again?
options: The page is evicted immediately
Its dirty flag is always cleared
pinCount increases to 2 and the frame address is returned
The page must be read from disk and the count set to 0
questions.explanation: A cache hit adds another user. It does not require rereading the page or erasing its dirty history.

questions.prompt: If dirty=true, what is the new dirty flag after unpin(page,false)?
options: false
Equal to pinCount
Undefined when cached
true
questions.explanation: The update uses OR. A false argument cannot clear an earlier modification.

questions.prompt: A cache miss selects an eligible dirty victim. What order is required?
options: Write the victim, then read the new page into the frame
Overwrite the frame with the new page, then write the victim from those same bytes
Discard the victim without writing it
Only increase the victim’s pinCount
questions.explanation: The modified contents must be preserved before the frame is overwritten. Reversing the order loses the bytes that need writing.

questions.prompt: After a miss loads a new page, how does the pseudocode initialise pinCount and dirty?
options: 0 and false
1 and false
0 and true
1 and true
questions.explanation: The caller has pinned the newly loaded page, and the freshly read contents have not been modified. A count of 0 would ignore that user.

questions.prompt: If two callers pin the same page, does the buffer manager automatically prevent conflicting writes?
options: Yes; the dirty flag makes every write atomic
Yes; a clean page forbids all writes
No; concurrency control coordinates writes
Yes; the pin count is an exclusive lock
questions.explanation: Pinning protects against replacement. It does not replace concurrent-access control.

questions.prompt: In the deck’s LRU model, when is the latest-use time primarily recorded?
options: Only when the page is first loaded, as in FIFO
Only when the page becomes dirty
Only when the page is flushed to disk
When the frame is unpinned
questions.explanation: The model uses the time when use ends. It should not be silently changed to FIFO’s load-time rule.

questions.prompt: A(pin=0,last=4), B(pin=1,last=1), C(pin=0,last=7). Which does LRU select?
options: A
B
C
No frame
questions.explanation: B is oldest but pinned. A is the oldest eligible frame.

questions.prompt: Two frames start empty and receive A,B,A,C, with immediate unpinning after each request. How many misses occur?
questions.explanation: A and B miss; the second A hits and updates recency; C misses and replaces B.

questions.prompt: Which management cost of exact LRU is mentioned in the lecture?
options: Increasing page size after every replacement
Synchronising every table’s schema at each unpin
Finding or maintaining the frame with the oldest use time
Sorting all on-disk records at every hit
questions.explanation: Maintaining recency order has overhead. This is not sorting the business data.

questions.prompt: Do LRU and FIFO always select the same victim?
options: Yes, because both use time
Yes, if the pages are clean
Yes, if frames hold integers
No; a hit changes recency without changing load time
questions.explanation: Reaccessing a page changes its recency history. FIFO still uses its original arrival time.

questions.prompt: What does CLOCK first do when it encounters an unpinned frame with ref=1?
options: Clear ref to 0 and continue
Evict immediately regardless of ref
Increase the pin count and stop
Write every page in the pool
questions.explanation: A page with ref=1 gets another chance. An eligible victim is unpinned and has ref=0 when examined.

questions.prompt: May CLOCK select a pinned frame with ref=0 as a victim?
options: Yes, if it is clean
No
Yes, because ref=0
Yes, after the hand completes a full revolution
questions.explanation: pinCount=0 remains mandatory. The reference bit cannot override that safety condition.

questions.prompt: A,B,C are all unpinned, with ref values 1,0,1. The hand starts at A. Which is the first victim?
options: C
None
B
A
questions.explanation: CLOCK clears A’s reference bit and moves on. B already has ref=0 and is selected.

questions.prompt: When is the reference bit set in the lecture’s model?
options: Only when the page is written back
Only when the pin count reaches 0 and the page is dirty
Only when CLOCK selects the page as a victim
When the pin count increases
questions.explanation: The bit records page use. It does not depend on a particular SQL clause.

questions.prompt: After a victim is replaced to serve a pin request, what is the correct state?
options: The new page is pinned with ref=1, and the hand advances
The new page is unpinned with ref=0, and the hand never moves
The new page is dirty by default because it was read
The old page’s nonzero pin count is retained
questions.explanation: The page is serving a caller, so it is pinned and referenced. Reading it does not automatically make it dirty.

topics.title: REPLACEMENT POLICIES CAN FAIL / REPEATED SCAN

questions.prompt: Three empty frames scan A,B,C twice using LRU and immediate unpinning. What is the total miss count?
questions.explanation: The working set fits in the pool. The first pass has three misses and the second consists entirely of hits.

questions.prompt: Three empty frames scan A,B,C,D twice using LRU and immediate unpinning. What is the total miss count?
questions.explanation: Each page has been evicted before its next use. A working set just one page larger than the pool causes flooding.

questions.prompt: Three frames contain A,B,C after a scan with immediate unpinning. Which page does MRU replace when loading D?
options: A
B
No page can be replaced
C
questions.explanation: C was used most recently. LRU would choose A in this state.

questions.prompt: What additional information does LRU-K use beyond the most recent access?
options: The history of the K most recent references
Only the time a page entered the pool, as in FIFO
Only the latest reference, discarding all older history
Only total access frequency, without K-th recency
questions.explanation: It considers deeper reference history, rather than only a page’s dirty state or name.

questions.prompt: What do the LRU and MRU examples teach about different workloads?
options: CLOCK does not need pin counts
Replacement effectiveness depends on the access pattern
MRU is better for every workload
LRU is always absolutely optimal
questions.explanation: Sequential scans and repeated access to hot pages behave differently. Neither policy wins in every case.

topics.title: BUFFER MANAGEMENT IN PRACTICE / WHY NOT USE THE OS?

questions.prompt: Why can a priority hint from the execution engine be useful?
options: It replaces the pinCount=0 requirement for eviction
It makes every page read require no I/O
The engine knows an operator’s upcoming access pattern
The engine knows every future access perfectly
questions.explanation: Workload information can guide replacement. It does not guarantee an unlimited cache.

questions.prompt: What are partitioned buffer pools?
options: Complete copies of every table in each frame
One OS process per tuple
A requirement that data and index pages share exactly one frame
Separate pools for object groups such as tables, indexes, or logs
questions.explanation: This partitions cache resources. It does not require copying all stored data.

questions.prompt: Which two activities can prefetch overlap?
options: I/O for upcoming pages and CPU processing of the current page
Flushing a page before any of its writes have occurred
Reading the whole database before any CPU work starts
Sorting records in RAM while eliminating all I/O
questions.explanation: The goal is to reduce waiting by overlapping computation and I/O, not to change the schema.

questions.prompt: Why does a DBMS want to control flush order?
options: To ensure the optimiser never has to choose a plan
Recovery may require writes to occur in an appropriate order
To change tuple order in every SQL result
To eliminate all concurrency control
questions.explanation: Durability and recovery depend on persistence order. Flushing must not change query results.

questions.prompt: Is prefetching a very large number of pages guaranteed to be optimal?
options: Yes; prefetch does not occupy buffer frames
Yes; speculative I/O uses no bandwidth
No; it can fetch unused pages and consume cache space
Yes; every prefetched page must be used immediately
questions.explanation: This follows from the trade-off: incorrect predictions create I/O and cache pressure. Prefetching is not free.
